headline: Connecticut officials question ICE arrests at Tweed, Bradley airports
dek: A New Haven briefing focused on recent detentions at the state's two major airports, including a Southern Connecticut State University basketball player later released from custody.
body: Connecticut elected officials and immigration advocates are challenging recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests at Tweed New Haven Airport and Bradley International Airport, saying the detentions reflect a widening federal presence in public spaces.

Connecticut Public, reporting from the Connecticut Mirror, said four young people had been detained at the two airports during the prior three weeks. Two were detained at Tweed and two at Bradley, according to U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who met with the group on Sept. 28. One of them was Deng Dhieu Kuach Deng, a South Sudan-born Southern Connecticut State University freshman basketball player who was detained Sept. 4 while trying to take a domestic flight from Tweed and released Sept. 16.

An Ecuadorian student from Fairfield County was also detained this month and released weeks later, the report said. Attorney Glenn Formica said the people involved spent roughly two to three weeks in ICE detention and generally do not receive the same court-appointed-counsel protections as people held on criminal charges. Those points were presented by the attorney and officials at the briefing, not as findings by the airport or ICE.

New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker said he asked the airport authority board to limit cooperation with ICE to what federal law requires. ICE did not respond to the Connecticut Mirror's requests for comment about the recent cases, while a separate agency statement defended the detention of the Southern Connecticut student and said people in the country illegally receive due process.

The airport arrests come after a four-day ICE operation centered in Danbury produced more than 100 arrests in August, according to the report. The latest briefing broadened the debate over where immigration enforcement occurs in Connecticut, as officials and advocates also point to activity near courthouses, streets and school transportation routes.
author: NorthEast News Desk
